content.title: FOOD FACTS THAT SOUND MADE UP (BUT ARE 100% REAL)
facts: **Nutmeg** – in large enough doses, this common baking spice is a hallucinogen that can cause vomiting, rapid heartbeat, and hours of delirium. A few teaspoons is the danger zone.
**Cashews** are never sold in their shell to consumers — the shell contains a resin related to poison ivy, and raw cashews must be steamed first to neutralize it.
**Carrots** were originally purple, not orange — orange carrots were selectively bred in the Netherlands centuries ago, reportedly in honor of the royal House of Orange.
**Black pepper** was once worth so much it was used as currency to pay rent and dowries in medieval Europe, earning the nickname 'black gold.'
**Strawberries** aren't technically berries, but bananas are — botanically speaking, a 'true berry' needs seeds inside its flesh, which bananas have and strawberries don't.
**Lettuce** is a distant relative of sunflowers — both belong to the same plant family, which is why some lettuce varieties sprout small yellow flowers if left to grow.
**Vanilla** is the second most expensive spice in the world after saffron, because each orchid flower must be hand-pollinated within hours of blooming or it produces nothing.
**Apples** float in water because they're about 25% air by volume — that trapped air is also why bobbing for apples actually works.
**Cranberries** bounce — ripe, high-quality ones literally bob like tiny rubber balls, a trick farmers still use to sort out the unripe ones.

content.caption:
The nutmeg fact genuinely surprises people — the compound responsible, myristicin, is metabolized by your liver into something structurally similar to amphetamine, which is why just a tablespoon or two can trigger real psychoactive effects for up to 24 hours. With cashews, that poison-ivy-related resin (urushiol) sits between the shell and the nut itself, so commercial processing uses steam specifically to break it down before you ever see the nut in a bag. And vanilla's hand-pollination problem exists because the plant that produces it only naturally flowers for about 24 hours a year outside of Madagascar's native bee and hummingbird range — no pollinator, no vanilla pod. Food chemistry is wild once you look closely, and everyone's body reacts a little differently to compounds like these, so always respect the ones that come with real warnings.
